chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from some of his companions; and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas'ada ibn Sadaqa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him); and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Mahbub, who raised it (marfu') from Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him), that he said:

Indeed, among the most hateful of creatures to God, Mighty and Majestic, are two men. A man whom God has left to himself — he is biased away from the straight course, enamored of the speech of innovation (bid'ah); he has become engrossed in fasting and prayer, yet he is a trial for those who are tempted by him; straying from the guidance of those who came before him; leading astray those who follow him in his lifetime and after his death; bearing the sins of others and pledged by his own sin. And a man who has gathered up ignorance among the ignorant of the people, submerged in the darknesses of strife; people resembling scholars have named him a scholar, yet he has not been sound in it even for a single complete day. He rose early and accumulated much of what little of it is better than much —

until when he had drunk his fill from stagnant water and stored up from that which has no benefit, he sat among the people as a judge, guaranteeing to clarify what had become confused for others. If he opposes a judge who preceded him, he cannot be secure that his ruling will not be overturned by one who comes after him, just as he did to the one before him. And if one of the ambiguous, intractable matters descends upon him, he concocts stuffing for it from his own opinion and then issues a definitive ruling on it. So he is, in his wearing of obscurities, like the web of a spider — he does not know whether he has hit the mark or erred. He does not reckon that there is knowledge in anything he has denied, nor does he see that behind what he has reached there is a school of thought. If he compares something to something, he does not doubt his own view.

And if a matter becomes obscure to him, he conceals it because he knows of his own ignorance, lest it be said of him that he does not know; then he becomes bold and passes judgment. So he is a key to darknesses, a rider upon obscurities, a blunderer through ignorances. He does not excuse himself from what he does not know so that he might be saved, nor does he bite into knowledge with a cutting molar so that he might profit. He scatters the narrations as the wind scatters dry grass. The inheritances weep because of him and the bloodshed cries out because of him. By his ruling, the forbidden private part is made permissible and the permissible private part is made forbidden. He is not capable of issuing rulings on what comes to him, nor is he worthy of what he overreaches in his claim to knowledge of the truth.

key_terms.الرَّأْي: Personal opinion — legal reasoning based on one's own view rather than revelation
key_terms.الشُّبُهَات: Obscurities/ambiguities — matters that are unclear and require proper scholarly grounding to resolve
key_terms.الْفَرْج: The private part — used in jurisprudence to refer to marriage/sexual permissibility rulings
key_terms.الْهَشِيم: Dry, crumbled vegetation — a metaphor for scattered, incoherent narrations
key_terms.بِدْعَة: Innovation (bid'ah) — introducing into religion what has no basis in revelation or the Imams' teaching
key_terms.فِتْنَة: Trial/sedition — a person or thing that causes others to deviate from truth
key_terms.قَاضِي: Judge — one who issues binding legal rulings
key_terms.قِيَاس: Analogy — comparing new cases to precedents, condemned here as a method of independent legal reasoning

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Ali say about the two most hated men before God?
ai.summary: In this extended warning narrated through two chains reaching Imam Ali (AS) and Imam al-Sadiq (AS), Imam Ali describes the two types of men most hated by God: the religiously deluded innovator who, abandoned by God to himself, leads others astray through his piety-garbed bid'ah; and the fake scholar who gathered superficial knowledge among the ignorant, gained an undeserved reputation, and then sat in judicial authority — making catastrophic errors in legal rulings affecting marriage and blood while unable to acknowledge his own ignorance. The hadith is a cornerstone text in Shia epistemology condemning unauthorized religious opinion (ra'y) and legal analogy (qiyas).
